# Power truncation for symmetric concave sequences, and the linear obstruction

Let N>=0, r_0=R>0, R>=r_1>=...>=r_N>=0, and

    r_(k-1)-r_k <= r_k-r_(k+1)  for 1<=k<N.

Extend symmetrically by r_(-k)=r_k and write

    Q_p(c)=sum_(k=-N)^N (r_k-c)_+^p,  0<=c<=R,
    (x)_+=max(x,0).

For EVERY real p>=2,

    Q_p(c) >= (1-c/R)^(p+1) Q_p(0)
                   +c(R-c)^p/[R(2N+1)].         (1)

In particular the requested inequality without the remainder holds
for every integer d=p>=2, with the exact exponent d+1, and is strict
for 0<c<R. The proposed assertion for all integer d>=1 is false:
an exact counterexample at d=1 is given in Section 3.

The power moment inequality used here already appears in
`candidate 273393b2aa6803aa`; the present result
is its truncation normalization and application, not a new moment
theorem. The stronger nonsymmetric truncation version, retaining
the exact peak-block correction, is in
`candidate c3c2ca0e4dcbdc9d`.

The proof uses only a finite sequence and one integral of elementary
powers. It does not assume that sampling a continuously concave
function preserves any unproved measure inequality.

## 1. The audited quadratic input in difference form

The proved theorem in
`candidate ff51b2f45de7ad0e`, independently
audited in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`,
gives for

    F_2(c)=Q_2(c)/(R-c)^3,  0<=c<R,

the derivative inequality

    F_2'(c)>=1/[(2N+1)(R-c)^2].                 (2)

That derivative exists and is continuous even at truncation knots.
Integrating (2) between arbitrary 0<=a<b<R gives

    F_2(b)-F_2(a)
      >=[1/(R-b)-1/(R-a)]/(2N+1).              (3)

For p=2, (1) is precisely the audited quadratic theorem. It remains
to prove the extension p>2.

## 2. Integral lifting to every real power p>2

Put C_p=p(p-1)(p-2)/2. For s>=0, direct integration gives

    C_p integral_0^s t^(p-3)(s-t)^2 dt=s^p.     (4)

Indeed the coefficient after expanding the square is
1/(p-2)-2/(p-1)+1/p=2/[p(p-1)(p-2)]. This calculation is valid
for p>2; the power t^(p-3) is integrable at zero. Apply (4) to
each s=(r_k-c)_+, sum the FINITELY many terms, and extend each
integral to R-c using its positive part. This yields

    Q_p(c)=C_p integral_0^(R-c)
                          t^(p-3) Q_2(c+t) dt. (5)

For c<R set h=R-c, substitute t=hs, and divide by h^(p+1).
Writing F_p(c)=Q_p(c)/(R-c)^(p+1), equation (5) becomes

    F_p(c)=C_p integral_0^1 s^(p-3)(1-s)^3
                           F_2(c+(R-c)s) ds.   (6)

All these integrals exist. Near s=0 the weight s^(p-3) is
integrable, and for any t<R

    Q_2(t)<=(2N+1)(R-t)^2,
    F_2(t)<=(2N+1)/(R-t).

Thus the integrand in (6) is bounded by
[(2N+1)/(R-c)] s^(p-3)(1-s)^2, integrable also at s=1.
The value at the single endpoint s=1 need not be assigned to F_2.

Fix 0<=c_0<c_1<R and put h_i=R-c_i. For 0<=s<1 define
t_i=c_i+h_i s. Then t_0<t_1<R and R-t_i=h_i(1-s).
Applying (3) pointwise gives

    F_2(t_1)-F_2(t_0)
       >=[1/h_1-1/h_0]/[(2N+1)(1-s)].          (7)

Multiply by the nonnegative integrable weight in (6), and integrate.
Subtraction of the two integrals is legitimate by the preceding
absolute integrability bound. Another instance of (4), at s=1,
gives

    C_p integral_0^1 s^(p-3)(1-s)^2 ds=1.

Consequently

    F_p(c_1)-F_p(c_0)
          >=[1/(R-c_1)-1/(R-c_0)]/(2N+1).      (8)

No differentiation under an improper integral, exchange of an
infinite sum, or interpolation of sampled radii was used.

Take c_0=0 and c_1=c<R, and multiply (8) by (R-c)^(p+1).
Its first term is (1-c/R)^(p+1)Q_p(0), and its remainder is

    (R-c)^(p+1)[1/(R-c)-1/R]/(2N+1)
        =c(R-c)^p/[R(2N+1)].

This proves (1). At c=0 the assertion is equality. At c=R all
terms vanish, so this endpoint is valid directly. The positive
remainder proves strictness of the assertion without a remainder
whenever 0<c<R. For N=0 the full strengthened assertion is an
identity for all c, since
(R-c)^(p+1)/R+c(R-c)^p/R=(R-c)^p.

For comparison, the already archived moment inequality for every
real p>=2 can also be recovered as

    (p+1) sum r_k^p -pR sum r_k^(p-1)
                         >=R^p/(2N+1).         (9)

To obtain it, take the right derivative of (8) at c_0=c_1=0.
For p>=2, each positive-part power is continuously differentiable
at its zero, and zero endpoint radii contribute zero to that
derivative. Thus F_p'(0) is exactly the left side of (9), divided
by R^(p+2); the right derivative of the lower bound in (8) is
1/[(2N+1)R^2]. This proves (9), with no convention for 0^0.

## 3. Exact counterexample at the integer power d=1

Set N=1, R=1, and r_1=1/3. The symmetric sequence is

    (r_-1,r_0,r_1)=(1/3,1,1/3).

It satisfies every stated hypothesis; the one-sided concavity
condition for 1<=k<N is empty when N=1, and the full symmetric
sequence is also discretely concave at its center. At c=1/3,

    Q_1(c)=2/3=18/27,
    (1-c/R)^2 Q_1(0)=(2/3)^2(5/3)=20/27.

Thus the desired inequality at d=1 fails by exactly 2/27. This
does not depend on using a truncation knot: at c=1/4 the left
side is 11/12=44/48, while the proposed right side is
(3/4)^2(5/3)=15/16=45/48, a failure of 1/48.

The valid N=1 examples already refute the asserted all-integer-power
formulation. They do not refute (OC), whose geometric hypotheses
and center choice are different.
